Rebekah · Genesis 24:12-21

A Woman of Formidable Strength

From The God Who Hears Her by Dr. Connie Champeon · 5 min read

“O LORD, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham. Here I am, standing beside the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water. Now may it happen that the girl to whom I say, ‘Please let down your jar that I may drink,’ and who responds, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well’—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I will know that You have shown kindness to my master.”

“Before the servant had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor. Now the girl was very beautiful, a virgin who had not had relations with any man. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again. So the servant ran to meet her and said, “Please let me have a little water from your jar.”

“Drink, my lord,” she replied, and she quickly lowered her jar to her hands and gave him a drink. After she had given him a drink, she said, “I will also draw water for your camels, until they have had enough to drink.” And she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran back to the well to draw water, until she had drawn water for all his camels. Meanwhile, the man watched her silently to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success.” (Genesis 24:12-21)

Abraham’s servant Eliezer has sworn to his master he will travel 450-500 miles, about 30 days by camel, to a place he may never have been or at least hasn’t been since he was a young man. He knows no one, but he is supposed to find a wife for Isaac. What woman worthy of being a keeper of the Covenant is going to be willing to leave her family and go with a stranger to marry a stranger and never see her family again? He is looking for a needle in a haystack. So he asks God for what seems like an impossible sign. Eliezer asks God to show him a woman who will choose* something instantly, for a stranger, at real cost to herself.

This is one of sixty devotions through the women of Genesis.

Why was this such a costly thing to offer? A camel could have needed as much as 20-30 gallons of water to drink, so she’d need to offer to carry about 250 gallons of water. At about 8.3 pounds per gallon that is 2,075 pounds of water, literally the weight of a small car. A typical water jar in the Ancient Near East held about 3 gallons, so that is 83 trips down to the well. The jar weighs about 10-15 pounds when empty so full it’s about 35-40 pounds. Usually the wells were actually springs, and the townspeople would dig a shallow stone pool with steps going down into it. So Rebekah climbed those steps again and again. Down with 10-15 pounds (6 kilograms) in her arms. Up with 35-40 pounds (18 Kilograms). Down and up, down and up. A soldier in training would feel it. So Rebekah was doing an intense, stair-climbing exercise like someone might do to get in top shape while carrying 10-15 pounds down and 35-40 back up. Assuming the well wasn’t that deep and the steps were well-maintained, each 3-gallon jar would take 1.5-2 minutes, so she carried that weight up and down for two or three hours without stopping. Rebekah did not count the camels before she spoke. She volunteered for hours of work before she knew the man's name. She may well have had women with her since a household her size would not send its daughter to the well alone (We will come back to that aspect later.) However, the offer was hers, the first trips were hers, and the cost was hers to carry. That is what Eliezer sat and watched in silence. He was in awe I think. Don’t we all pray impossible prayers, and then sit in awe when God answers? At least, that should be our response! He asked the God of Abraham to show him the kind of woman who could build a nation, and God answered.

In many translations of Proverbs 31, the word used to describe the wife is 'virtuous.' For most of us, that brings to mind a woman who is quiet, chaste, and morally pure. But the original Hebrew word doesn't mean passive goodness at all; it means 'formidable' and speaks to us of action. Hayil (חַיִל) usually refers to military force or mighty warriors. In Exodus 18:21, Jethro tells Moses to look for "men of hayil," men of strength and substance to help lead the people. It is also the word used for Pharaoh’s army that chases the Israelites into the Red Sea. It is the word used multiple times in Joshua for “mighty men of valor” (Joshua 6:2; 8:3; 10:7). It is the word the angel uses to describe Gideon. It is used over 200 times in the Hebrew Bible, but it was only translated as “virtuous” three times. Those three times all describe women. (It seems like some translators have assumed that the Hebrew authors of Ruth and Proverbs did not intend to discuss women of strength, substance, and valor! But I digress, Proverbs 31 is still a long way away.)

Rebekah displays this formidable competence and strength that will later be codified in Proverbs. “She arms her waist with strength, and makes her arms strong.” (Pro 31:17) I asked AI what Rebekah would have looked like based on what the Bible says and archeology from that place and time period. It obliged by producing an image including Eliezer’s gift of the nose ring; that definitely confronts our cultural perceptions with what the text actually says. The image made her more tangible and real, like a woman with whom I’d love to spend some time. Studying Rebekah fills my heart. She was a strong woman who launched out on an incredible journey of faith. She didn’t know using her strength to help this stranger would change the course of her life. She just did it because of the kind of person she was. But God had created her to be the kind of woman Isaac would need to build the nation of His Covenant people. I’m facing a calling right now that frequently has me feeling pretty small and unable. Rebekah’s story is a powerful reminder not to doubt that God has given me the strength for this specific assignment. It challenges me to unapologetically be exactly who He designed me to be and to serve with boldness, passion, and faith.

—-

*Note: The name Eliezer contains the same word “ezer” that we have been discussing since Genesis 2. His name means “My God is help” or “God is my strength.” Abraham's trusted manager is a literal "man of ezer," who journeys to find Rebekah — a woman who will embody that very same ezer strength to sustain the future of the Covenant family.
